sections.b: Kings gives Hezekiah the highest praise it gives any king for trust: none before or after him was like him (2 Kings 18:5). He removes the high places and breaks the bronze snake (18:4), rebels against Assyria (18:7), and when Sennacherib invades, first pays tribute (18:14–16) and then, faced with the Rabshakeh's taunts, turns to the LORD and to Isaiah (19:1–4, 19:14–19). Jerusalem is spared (19:35–36). Sick to death, he prays and weeps and is given fifteen more years (20:1–11); then he shows his treasures to the envoys of Babylon and hears that they will be taken there (20:12–19).

Sennacherib's annals name "Hezekiah the Judean" as the rebel he shut up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage," listing 46 of his walled towns taken and a large tribute. The reliefs of Lachish show one of those towns falling. In Jerusalem, the Siloam tunnel and its inscription, the "Broad Wall" in the Jewish Quarter and royal storage jars stamped lmlk ("belonging to the king") are widely linked with his preparations for the war. A clay seal impression reading "belonging to Hezekiah son of Ahaz, king of Judah" was found in the Ophel excavations in 2015.

common: Hezekiah is remembered as one of Judah's two great reforming kings, with Josiah.
uncommon: Some historians think Hezekiah's rebellion was a disaster for Judah and that the praise of Kings hides how much the country lost in 701.

claude.title: A king of two moods
claude.body: Kings presents Hezekiah in pairs: the trusting king (18:5) and the frightened tributary (18:14); the king whose prayer saves the city (19:15–19) and the king who boasts to Babylon (20:13). The pairing may be meant: trust is not a fixed trait but something Hezekiah must choose again in each crisis, and the narrator does not hide the times he did not. Commentators have often contrasted 18:5 with 18:14; the suggestion that the pairs are a deliberate pattern running through all three chapters is Claude's reading, and may have been made elsewhere.

sections.b: Sennacherib's third campaign is one of the best-documented events in the Old Testament. Kings, Isaiah and Chronicles tell it from Jerusalem (2 Kings 18:13–19:37; Isaiah 36–37; 2 Chronicles 32:1–23); Sennacherib's annals tell it from Nineveh, and the reliefs of his palace show the siege of Lachish. Both sides agree that Judah's towns fell, that Hezekiah paid tribute, and that Jerusalem was not taken. Kings says the angel of the LORD struck the camp (2 Kings 19:35); the annals say only that Hezekiah sent his tribute to Nineveh. Sennacherib was killed by his son around 681 BC (2 Kings 19:37), and Esarhaddon succeeded him.

After Sennacherib, Assyria held Judah as a vassal under Manasseh, whom Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal name in their lists of tributary kings. When Assyria weakened in the 620s, Josiah's reform reached into the old northern provinces (2 Kings 23:15–20). Nineveh fell in 612. In 609, Pharaoh Neco marched north to help the last Assyrian king at Harran, and killed Josiah on the way at Megiddo (2 Kings 23:29).

common: Assyria was destroyed for its pride, as Isaiah promised (Isaiah 10:12–19; 2 Kings 19:21–28).
uncommon: A few historians argue for a second campaign of Sennacherib against Judah around 688 BC, which they think lies behind 2 Kings 19:9–35.

sections.b: Manasseh reigned 55 years, longer than any king of Judah (2 Kings 21:1). Kings lists his sins as a kind of reverse of his father's reform: he rebuilt the high places, set up Baal altars and an Asherah, worshipped the army of the heavens in the temple courts, burned his son and consulted spirits (21:2–7), and filled Jerusalem with innocent blood (21:16). Unnamed prophets announced that Jerusalem would be wiped out like a bowl (21:10–15). Later chapters say Josiah's reform could not turn the anger his deeds had roused (23:26–27; 24:3–4).

sections.h: Manasseh in Chronicles and later tradition
sections.b: 2 Chronicles 33 adds that the Assyrians took Manasseh to Babylon in chains, where he humbled himself and prayed; God brought him back, and he removed the foreign gods. A short penitential "Prayer of Manasseh" was later written in his name and appears in many Greek, Latin and Slavonic Bibles. The Mishnah lists him among kings with no share in the world to come, but the Talmud records the view that his repentance was accepted.

common: Manasseh was the worst king of Judah, and his sins caused the exile (2 Kings 24:3–4).
uncommon: Some historians see Manasseh as a practical ruler who kept Judah at peace as Assyria's vassal, blamed by later writers for a disaster that came long after him.

sections.b: Josiah came to the throne at eight after his father Amon was murdered (2 Kings 21:23–22:1). In his eighteenth year a scroll of the law was found in the temple; when it was read to him he tore his clothes and sent to the prophet Huldah (22:3–20). He made a covenant with all the people, cleansed the temple, defiled the high places from Geba to Beersheba and the child-sacrifice site of Topheth, tore down the altar at Bethel as a man of God had foretold (1 Kings 13:2), and held a Passover like none since the judges (23:1–23). Kings says no king before or after him turned to the LORD so wholly (23:25). He was killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Neco in 609 BC (23:29).

sections.h: Josiah in Chronicles, Jeremiah and later tradition
sections.b: Chronicles places the start of his reform in his twelfth year, before the scroll was found, and says he died of arrow wounds after refusing Neco's warning (2 Chronicles 34:3–7; 35:20–25). Jeremiah began to prophesy in his thirteenth year and praises him as a king who judged the poor (Jeremiah 1:2; 22:15–16). Ben Sira remembers him as sweet as honey (Ben Sira 49:1–3).

common: Josiah's reform was guided by the scroll of Deuteronomy.
uncommon: Some scholars think the account of Josiah's reform was written up much later, and that his actual changes were small.

claude.title: Josiah as a new Joshua
claude.body: Several details make Josiah look like Joshua: a covenant read to all the people (2 Kings 23:2–3; Joshua 8:34–35; 24:25), a Passover unmatched "since the time of the judges" (2 Kings 23:22), the last one recorded before the judges being Joshua's at Gilgal (Joshua 5:10–11), a king who turns neither right nor left (2 Kings 22:2; Joshua 1:7), and a purge of the land's shrines that recalls the conquest. This parallel was set out by Richard D. Nelson (1981) and is widely discussed. Claude adds only that Josiah's death at Megiddo, a city Joshua defeated (Joshua 12:21), may be meant to close the circle, though the text does not say so.
claude.refs: 2 Kings 22:2; 2 Kings 23:2–3; 2 Kings 23:21–23; 2 Kings 23:29; Joshua 1:7; Joshua 5:10–11; Joshua 8:34–35; Joshua 12:21

sections.b: 2 Kings 18:4 is the snake's last appearance in the Old Testament. Hezekiah "crushed to pieces" the bronze snake Moses made, because the Israelites had been burning incense to it, and the narrator adds its popular name, Nehushtan. The Mishnah lists this among the acts the sages approved (Mishnah Pesahim 4:9). Many critical scholars think the image stood in the temple as a symbol of healing, perhaps linked to the winged serpents of Isaiah 6, and that its link to Moses may have been part of what made it honored.

sections.h: Hezekiah and Josiah close the high places
sections.b: Hezekiah is the first king of Judah said to have removed the high places (2 Kings 18:4), and the Rabshakeh turns this against him (18:22). Manasseh rebuilds them (21:3). Josiah defiles them from Geba to Beersheba, brings their priests to Jerusalem, and destroys the high places Solomon built for foreign gods and Jeroboam's altar at Bethel (23:8–9, 23:13, 23:15, 23:19). The country priests do not serve at the Jerusalem altar but eat unleavened bread with their brothers (23:9), a detail that seems to fall short of Deuteronomy 18:6–8.

Babylon enters Kings as a friend: Merodach-baladan's envoys visit sick Hezekiah, perhaps to recruit him against Assyria, and Isaiah announces that everything they saw will go to Babylon (2 Kings 20:12–19). A century later Nebuchadnezzar makes Jehoiakim a vassal, takes Jehoiachin and the treasures in 597, and burns Jerusalem in 586 (24:1–25:21). The book ends in Babylon, with Evil-merodach releasing Jehoiachin from prison (25:27–30).

2 Kings tells two deportations from Judah. In 597 Nebuchadnezzar took Jehoiachin, his mother and court, the soldiers and the craftsmen, 10,000 in one count, 7,000 soldiers and 1,000 craftsmen in another (2 Kings 24:14–16). In 586 Nebuzaradan burned Jerusalem and took the rest except the poorest, and the book sums it up: Judah went into exile from its own soil (25:11–12, 25:21). After Gedaliah's murder many fled to Egypt (25:26). Jeremiah 52:28–30 counts 4,600 in three deportations. Babylonian tablets name Jehoiachin as a royal captive, and the Al-Yahudu tablets show Judean families farming in Babylonia two generations later.

uncommon: Some historians think most of Judah's people were never deported, and that the "empty land" picture, given most fully in 2 Chronicles 36:20–21 and suggested by 2 Kings 25:26, reflects the exiles' view.

sections.h: Josiah's scroll and the end of the History
sections.b: The finding of the scroll in Josiah's temple (2 Kings 22:8) has been at the center of the theory since de Wette identified the scroll with Deuteronomy. Many scholars, following Frank Moore Cross, think a first edition of the History was written under Josiah and ended in his praise (23:25), and that a second edition after 586 added the verdict that his reform could not undo Manasseh's sins (23:26–27; 24:3–4) and the story of the fall. The last four verses (25:27–30) have been read as hope for David's line, as a closing epitaph, or as advice for life in exile.

sections.h: The scroll of the law found
sections.b: In 2 Kings 22:8 the high priest Hilkiah reports, "The scroll of the law! I have found it in the LORD's house." It is called "the covenant scroll" in 23:2 and "the law of Moses" in 23:25. Josiah reads it to all the people and makes them take their stand in its covenant (23:2–3). Its laws, as Josiah carried them out, are those of Deuteronomy: one altar, no mediums, Passover at the chosen place. Kings had already praised Hezekiah for keeping "the LORD's commands, the ones he gave Moses" (18:6).

Josiah's Passover is held in Jerusalem, "by what is written in this covenant scroll" (2 Kings 23:21), and the narrator says no Passover like it had been held since the judges (23:22). The newness is probably that it was kept at the one chosen place, as Deuteronomy 16:5–7 requires, rather than in homes. 2 Chronicles 35:1–19 gives it much more detail, and 2 Chronicles 30 tells of an earlier Passover under Hezekiah, which Kings does not mention.

Manasseh "made his son pass through the fire" (2 Kings 21:6), as Ahaz had (16:3). Josiah defiled Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom so that no one could make a son or daughter pass through the fire for Molech there (23:10). Jeremiah names the same place and says the people burned their children there (Jeremiah 7:31; 19:5–6). Whether "Molech" names a god or a kind of offering, and whether the practice was sacrifice or dedication, is discussed on this page.

Isaiah's oracle in 2 Kings 19:21–34 is one of the Bible's key texts for the belief that God defends Zion. Daughter Zion laughs at Sennacherib (19:21), a remnant goes out from Mount Zion (19:31), and God promises to shield the city for his own sake and David's (19:34). The rescue of 701 seemed to confirm the belief, which Jeremiah later warned against trusting blindly (Jeremiah 7:4; 26:18–19).

claude.title: Why Zion survived 701 and fell in 586
claude.body: Kings itself holds the answer it gives to the puzzle of why the same city was spared under Hezekiah and burned under Zedekiah: the city was shielded for God's own sake and David's (2 Kings 19:34; 20:6), and the narrator treats Manasseh's sins as cancelling that protection (24:3–4). The theology of Zion in Kings is therefore conditional, closer to Jeremiah than to the Psalms. A conditional reading of Zion's protection in Kings is close to R. E. Clements's argument in Isaiah and the Deliverance of Jerusalem; Claude's emphasis is only that Kings itself, not just Jeremiah, makes the condition.

sections.b: Hezekiah prays twice in 2 Kings. With Sennacherib's letter spread out before the LORD in the temple, he prays that God will save Jerusalem so that all the kingdoms of the earth will know that he alone is God (2 Kings 19:14–19); the answer comes through Isaiah (19:20). On his sickbed he turns his face to the wall and weeps, and God answers, "I have heard your prayer. I have seen your tears" (20:2–5). Isaiah 38:9–20 adds a song of thanks he wrote after his recovery. Josiah's grief over the scroll, which Huldah says God has heard (22:19), is a third.

In 2 Kings 19:35 the angel of the LORD goes out by night and strikes 185,000 in the Assyrian camp. The picture recalls the destroyer of Egypt's firstborn (Exodus 12:23) and the angel with a drawn sword over Jerusalem in David's census (2 Samuel 24:16). The text names no means. Readers have taken it as a direct miracle, as a plague in the camp, or as a theological way of telling the rescue; Ben Sira and 1 Maccabees remember it as God's great deliverance (Ben Sira 48:21; 1 Maccabees 7:41).

Hezekiah's prayer (2 Kings 19:15–19) is among the clearest statements of monotheism in Kings: the LORD alone is God over every kingdom on earth and made the heavens and the earth, while the gods of the nations Assyria destroyed were "no gods at all," only wood and stone made by human hands. The language is close to Deuteronomy 4:28 and to Isaiah 40–46.

sections.h: The last king of David's line
sections.b: Kings tests the promise to David at its end. God shields Jerusalem "for David my servant's sake" (2 Kings 19:34; 20:6). The kings after Josiah lose their throne one by one: Jehoahaz to Egypt, Jehoiachin to Babylon, Zedekiah blinded at Riblah after watching his sons die (23:33–34; 24:15; 25:7). The book ends with Jehoiachin alive in Babylon and honored above other captive kings (25:27–30). Jeremiah had said no son of his would sit on David's throne (Jeremiah 22:30); his grandson Zerubbabel later led the return, and Matthew traces Jesus through him (Matthew 1:12).

sections.b: About three hundred years after the man of God from Judah spoke against Jeroboam's altar, Josiah burns bones from the Bethel tombs on it and so defiles it, "just as the LORD's word had said" (2 Kings 23:15–16). Seeing a grave marker, he learns it belongs to that man of God, and orders his bones left alone, with the bones of the old prophet from Samaria buried beside him (23:17–18; 1 Kings 13:31–32).

Manasseh places a carved image of Asherah in the temple and serves idols (2 Kings 21:7, 21:11, 21:21). Josiah's purge removes every object made for Baal, Asherah and the army of the heavens, burns them in the Kidron and scatters their dust (23:4–6), takes away the sun's horses and chariots (23:11), and sweeps away the household gods and idols (23:24).

Manasseh read signs, looked for omens and appointed people to deal with the ghosts of the dead and the spirits that know things (2 Kings 21:6), almost exactly the practices listed in Deuteronomy 18:10–11. Josiah swept them away as a final act of his reform (2 Kings 23:24).

The temple is stripped by Hezekiah to pay Sennacherib (2 Kings 18:15–16), filled with Manasseh's altars and an image of Asherah (21:4–7), repaired and cleansed by Josiah (22:3–7; 23:4–12), plundered in 597 (24:13), and burned by Nebuzaradan in 586 (25:9). Its bronze pillars, Sea and stands, described when Solomon made them (1 Kings 7:15–47), are broken up and carried to Babylon (25:13–17).

Jerusalem grew greatly in the late 8th century, and many think refugees from the north and from Judah's ruined towns filled its new western quarter, though the date and cause of the growth are debated; the Broad Wall and the Siloam tunnel date from this time (2 Kings 20:20). It survived Sennacherib in 701 (19:32–36) and surrendered to Nebuchadnezzar in 597 (24:10–12). In 586 its walls were broken, its houses burned and its people taken away (25:1–11). Archaeology in the City of David shows the burnt layer of that destruction.

2 Kings 18:9–12 repeats the fall of Samaria in Hezekiah's sixth year and the deportation of Israel to Halah, the Habor and the towns of the Medes. 2 Chronicles 30 says Hezekiah later invited the remnant of the northern tribes to Passover in Jerusalem, and Josiah's reform reached the towns of Samaria (2 Kings 23:19–20).
